newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian PM stands by land rights compromise.
newsitem.headline: Australian PM stands by land rights compromise.

text.p: Australian Prime Minister John Howard on Thursday declared he would stick to his compromise plan to settle a national land rights dispute between farmers and Aborigines, despite criticism from both sides.

Howard said his plan gave Aborigines continued access to land while providing security to farmers and miners who say the land rights row is hurting their businesses, which earn Australia tens of billions of dollars a year in exports.

The conservative leader, struggling to resolve confusion over native title land rights sparked by a December High Court ruling, on Thursday spent several hours talking separately with Aborigines and politicians.
Asked in a radio interview if he would continue with his controversial 10-point plan, Howard said: "I certainly am.
"The plan I put forward represents a fair attempt by me and my government to do justice to the Aborigines because it doesn't involve blanket extinguishment of title," Howard said.
"It doesn't disrespect native title, but it does deliver security and predictability...it is a fair plan."
The central elements of Howard's compromise include confirming farmers' rights over their properties, but guaranteeing Aborigines access for traditional purposes.
It also reduces Aboriginal rights to negotiate over development and other uses of land and reportedly exempts cities, towns and water supplies.
Howard has said 78 percent of Australia's 7.68 million square km (2.96 million square miles) could be claimed by Aborigines under native title land laws.

Farmers and the rural-based National Party, the junior member of Howard's Liberal-National coalition government, want Aboriginal rights to government land leased for pastoral use to be abolished, or extinguished.
Farmers and Aborigines have threatened major court action once Howard's plan is formalised.

Miners and farmers have complained that uncertainty has crippled Australia's valuable primary industries since the High Court in December unexpectedly ruled that Aborigines had rights to land the government had let to farmers on long-term leases.
